text.p: Australian carrier Qantas Airways Ltd said on Thursday it plans to offer video games, movies and possibly gambling on its international flights as part of a A$560 million investment to compete with rival airlines.
"The airline market is so competitive, we have got to make this sort of investment," Strong told Reuters by telephone.
"If you look over the next five years all the major airlines are going to be doing this," Strong said.
Qantas plans to spend A$320 million on the interactive services, with the balance being spent on new seating.
However, Qantas has not being given the all clear from the government to install gaming facilities on its aircraft.
"The concerns to us is that we would not be able to offer this service, while a major competitor could do it," group executive general manager commercial Geoff Dixon told reporters.

"The business case does not include any gaming revenue, but it would very important for our bottom line, we do need gaming," Dixon said. He added the airline was in talks with state and federal governments, but there has been no agreement.

The airline had invited U.S. group Interactive Flight Technologies (IFT) to put in a tender to supply Qantas with the interactive system, Strong said. He added the system would not be installed until around April 1998.
IFT currently supply Swissair, while Singapore Airlines Ltd announced last year it would install interactive systems on its aircraft.

Strong said Qantas had held off making this investment before in order to wait for some of the bugs in the interactive system to be sorted out. He added there were no plans to use the gaming on domestic flights.
The planned investment is unlikely to affect Qantas's bottom line profit or its ability to cut costs, analysts said.
"I think this is just a sign of how tough the market is. They are doing this just to keep market share, never mind growing their market share," said one aviation analyst who asked not to be named.

Strong would not say what kinds of gambling were being discussed but added an unspecified maximum bet would be imposed. "I don't think anybody is specifically going to catch a flight in order to gamble," Strong said.
Australia is in the midst of a gambling boom with many local casinos looking to lure Asian high-roller.
The Qantas refurbishment, which also includes high technology seating and improved amenities, will be made on all 99 of Qantas jets over the next three years.
Qantas is 25 percent owned by British Airways Plc. The British carrier also plans interactive entertainment and information systems on its flights.
